manuscript_state: Working tree after author-voice and protocol revision
scope: Every in-text citation occurrence in the current manuscript. Source anchors are printed only in the Markdown map; this file stores their offsets and hashes in normalized PDF page text.
normalization: pypdf page.extract_text(); Unicode NFKC; split on whitespace and join with one ASCII space. Offsets are Python Unicode character offsets; pages are one-based.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Andriella et al. model assistance type, timing, and confidence [1]
Andriella et al. learn proactive assistance from user profiles and task state in a sequential memory game, jointly addressing assistance type, timing, and confidence [1].

evidence.explanation: The abstract identifies assistance selection, intervention timing and confidence in taking control as the learned decisions.
The request-time classifier associates assistance level, user profile and game state with the time of a help request. This supports the user/task information part of our sentence.
The evaluation section describes participants playing the game with Furhat and contrasts proactive and non-proactive robot assistance.

references.interpretation_limit: Supports the three decision dimensions and this particular game implementation. It does not establish a physiological trigger or validate the present HR-rise threshold.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Adjacent assembly work by Caiazzo et al. compares manual, collaborative, and guided collaborative conditions, with EEG used for workload assessment [2].

evidence.explanation: The abstract enumerates assembly without the robot, with the robot, and with the robot plus task guidance. Our word “manual” paraphrases the no-robot condition.
This identifies the source study’s sample size, retained here as context for interpreting its scope.
The abstract identifies EEG as the workload measurement; PDF p. 4 describes preprocessing and feature extraction. The scenarios concern collaboration/guidance, not a reported online EEG trigger.

references.interpretation_limit: The N=3 qualification is essential. This is adjacent assembly evidence, not a test of our timing policy. Unverified DOI and proceedings pagination are omitted from the bibliography.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Capponi et al. similarly find no clear RMSSD pattern across their assembly configurations and distinguish cognitive effort from stress [3].

evidence.explanation: In §4.2.1 the authors describe overlapping distributions without clear trends, and no significant evidence for their hypothesis from RMSSD or its signed-rank tests.
The background distinguishes task-related cognitive demand from stress and explains that their relationship depends on the person and situation.

references.interpretation_limit: The negative RMSSD finding is specific to these tasks/configurations. It does not mean every cardiac measure is uninformative or that physiological state has no relationship with workload.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: PACE uses action-completion estimates to coordinate proactive assistance [4].
PACE estimates action completion from hand movements and uses a learned policy to coordinate assistance during collaborative assembly [4].

evidence.explanation: The paper describes DTW with correlation analysis to estimate human progress; methods on PDF pp. 4–5 develop the action-completion estimator.
The learned policy coordinates robot assistance with estimated progress; the methods explain the policy formulation. This supports “learned policy,” without importing claims of superiority.
The task description and Figure 3 describe collaborative wooden-chair assembly, including joint transport and tool handovers. Right-hand position is recorded with motion capture.

references.interpretation_limit: This is hand-motion/task-progress assistance, not physiology-based assistance. PDF p. 1 is a MERL cover and p. 2 is blank; the actual article begins on PDF p. 3.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Hart describes the six NASA-TLX workload dimensions and the use of an unweighted overall score [5].

evidence.explanation: The background names the six subscales. These are the dimensions referred to in our manuscript.
The modifications discussion explains Raw TLX after removal of the weighting procedure.

references.interpretation_limit: Hart supports describing and qualifying an adaptation; it does not validate our particular seven-point items, scoring, or psychometric properties. The paper is from 2006, regardless of its 2026 NASA upload path.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Hostettler et al. adapt robot behavior to user distance while measuring pupil responses; direct pupil-driven adaptation is a future direction [6].

evidence.explanation: The study design explicitly limits the implemented adaptation input to distance so the authors can examine effects on proximity and pupil responses.
The measures section lists these as objective responses, alongside subjective questionnaires.
The surrounding paragraph presents adaptation to workload measured through real-time pupil dilation as a future direction, rather than the implemented control input.

references.interpretation_limit: Do not cite the paper as an implemented pupil-triggered assistance policy. Its table of possible human characteristics includes prior literature; that table alone is not evidence of what its own experiment implemented.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: A recent review distinguishes adaptation of robot motion from task-level decisions about timing, sequencing, and role allocation [7].
Karbouj et al.'s review of adaptive industrial HRC distinguishes motion, task, and control adaptations and identifies task-level timing and coordination as areas warranting further attention [7].

evidence.explanation: The discussion identifies motion, task and control layers and contrasts how much adaptation research concentrates on each.
The surrounding passage names timing/synchronization, sequencing and role allocation, and discusses resulting coordination costs.

references.interpretation_limit: This supports the taxonomy and the review authors’ emphasis. It does not establish that no earlier study made our particular comparison. First publication was December 2025; the issue/volume is 2026.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Korivand et al. develop physiological task-load prediction and Q-learning-based adjustment, while explicitly reporting that their recorded wristband data could not be integrated directly for real-time use [8].

evidence.explanation: Data collection uses two robot-speed scenarios, wristband recordings and post-task workload ratings; the preprocessing section describes the physiological records.
In §5.5 this parameter is robot speed; the section describes physiological prediction followed by Q-learning-based task-load adjustment.
The limitations paragraph explicitly explains why the collected wristband data could not be directly integrated for live application.

references.interpretation_limit: The limitation qualifies the implemented evidence. The framework should not be presented as a demonstrated end-to-end real-time wrist-triggered deployment.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Recent work uses tangrams for collaborative HRI and as a simplified assembly task [12, 9].
SensCogAR uses tangrams as a proxy for small-object assembly, manipulating the visibility of piece contours to vary task demand [9].

evidence.explanation: §4.2 explains that participants manipulate similarly sized geometric objects to match a reference image; this supports the assembly-proxy half of the joint introduction citation.
The following paragraph distinguishes fully visible contours in low-difficulty puzzles from partly obscured contours in high-difficulty puzzles.

references.interpretation_limit: Task rationale transfers at the level of spatial manipulation. Neither the validity of all nine current puzzles nor generalization to industrial assembly follows automatically. PDF p. 15 discusses task/context limitations.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Ojsteršek et al. personalize robot parameters using a preliminary skills test and analyze ECG recordings after the experiment [10].

evidence.explanation: The experimental sequence uses that test to adjust robot movement parameters to worker utilization before the three scenarios.
The measurement paragraph says ECG data were transferred to KUBIOS HRV Scientific for subsequent analysis. The same paragraph identifies the ECG hardware and electrodes.

references.interpretation_limit: Personalization and physiological measurement both occur, but the described ECG analysis is not the real-time control input. The PDF extraction repeats some layout text; locators refer to the actual PDF page.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Pereira et al.'s review documents heterogeneous workload measures and mixed cardiac findings across HRC studies [11].

evidence.explanation: The cardiac-measures synthesis contrasts studies with nonsignificant HRV differences and studies with condition-specific RMSSD differences.
The discussion describes variation in workload measures, tasks, environments and interacting variables.

references.interpretation_limit: We cite the review’s synthesis, not independently verified findings from every study it includes. It supplies no validation for our specific sensor, threshold or task.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Recent work uses tangrams for collaborative HRI and as a simplified assembly task [12, 9].
Tabatabaei et al. study gaze around robot failures during collaborative tangram solving [12].

evidence.explanation: §III.A describes seven physical pieces, a division of pieces between robot and participant, and 3D-printed task materials. This supports the collaborative-HRI half of the joint citation.
The abstract defines the gaze/failure question and describes programmed executional and decisional robot failures; the methods describe the task and failure manipulations.

references.interpretation_limit: This is a gaze-and-failure study, not a test of physiological or scheduled help. The local version is arXiv v1 of the accepted HRI paper, so its PDF page numbers differ from proceedings pagination.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Earlier work by Teo et al. uses individualized physiological workload markers to trigger aid during robot supervision, imposing aid later when it has not been triggered [13].

evidence.explanation: §2.4 constructs markers from individual single-/dual-task baselines, compares the workload index to a threshold, and requires repeated high samples before triggering assistance.
The experimental design allows a trigger during the first ten minutes; if none occurs, aid is imposed during the last five minutes.

references.interpretation_limit: The study uses personalized multimeasure workload logic in robot supervision. It does not establish our heart-rate-rise threshold or identical assistance mechanics. Online publication was 2017; journal issue 2018.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: A recent HRI workshop proposal by Thunberg et al. emphasizes the practical, ethical, and methodological tensions of the wizard's role [14].

evidence.explanation: The abstract says surfacing these tensions is the workshop’s goal; the subsequent three-page proposal lays out its agenda and planned elicitation of wizard experiences.

references.interpretation_limit: Supports identifying a methodological concern and research agenda. It is explicitly a workshop proposal, not completed empirical evidence or a validated operator protocol.

occurrences.manuscript_excerpt: Yang et al. compared workload-adaptive robotic suction with periodic support during surgical training [15].
Yang et al.'s surgical system uses EEG and eye tracking to inform adaptive suction, with a periodic comparator selected to approximate earlier observed assistance frequency [15].

evidence.explanation: Experiment 2’s algorithm description combines the physiological/eye-tracking streams in the workload-adaptive suction system and evaluates it with surgical trainees.
The experimental design explicitly contrasts workload-adaptive automation with periodic automation that does not consider current workload.
The next sentences explain that the periodic interval was estimated from prior observed suction frequency under the adaptive system.

references.interpretation_limit: This is the direct precedent that prevents a claim that the comparison itself is new. “Closest” is our assessment within the reviewed set, not proof from an exhaustive review. Online publication was 2022 despite the 2024 issue; the cached PDF is an author manuscript.
